posts.text:
$NBIS - our updated valuation after Q3

Nebius traded near $123 before the open after Q3. We cut revenue per active MW in our capacity model by about 10%, in line with peers like CoreWeave ($9–11m per MW).

Weighted value: ~$220 a share

Base: $271 (was $302)
• 1,750 MW active by end-2027 at $10.8m per MW
• FY2027 revenue of $12.4bn, inside the new $12–13bn outlook
• $6.3bn of FY2027 EBITDA at 16x; ~$4.1bn of equity raised through 2028

Bull: $343 (was $380)
• 2,100 MW, $15.6bn of revenue, and prepayments cover the build with no new equity

Bear: $54 (was $63)
• 1,300 MW and $8.1m per MW, so revenue lands at $7.8bn
• ~$17.5bn of equity raised at $95. Dilution, not EBITDA, drives this case.

What matters most
- Activation pace: every 250 MW is about $3bn of ARR
- Revenue per MW: new contracts at $20–25m per MW leave room above our base case
- Funding: $17–20bn of guided prepayments plus a new $3.5bn Citi facility
- Risk: capex guidance of ~$27bn for 2026 and $40–45bn for 2027 is above what our model assumes.

At ~$123, the market is pricing our bear case’s funding stress, not the base case’s operating path.

Subscribers get the full interactive model.

Still, $NVDA is the best computing platform and ecosystem in the world. That won't change overnight no matter who's CEO. Platforms and ecosystems have staying power, just as $AAPL demonstrated when Tim Cook took over.

There is no replacing Jensen as an executive, but the board must find someone who can push the company with the same sense of relentless innovation that allowed them to defy the odds time and time again and remain on top for more than two decades. posts.text:
Despite all the negative feedback I got for saying on Monday the $NVDA Board would force Jensen Huang out as CEO, Huang resigned this morning and named CFO Collette Kress interim CEO until they find a replacement.  NVDA named veteran board member Harvey Jones (33 years on the $NVDA board) as Chairman. 

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns -- 4th Update

By Robbie Whelan, Josh Dawsey and Amrith Ramkumar 

11/12/2026 08:27:58 [WSJ]
(Wall Street Journal) -- Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has resigned after two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee. 

The company said Thursday that finance chief Colette Kress had agreed to serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. The board is starting a search for the company's next CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. 
Nvidia's board also appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones to become its first ever chair. Jones, a venture investor and technology executive, joined Nvidia's board in 1993, the year the company was founded. 

Kress, who will keep her role as CFO, said as part of the announcement that she is "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." 

Jones added that Kress is supported by an "experienced leadership team" and that the board expects to continue operations and its product roadmap "without interruption." 
Huang's resignation brings down the curtain on an era during which he stoked the global artificial-intelligence boom and became a geopolitical star. It leaves one of the world's most valuable companies in need of a new leader. Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia, is seen by many as the face of the AI arms race. 

Known for his leather jackets and near-constant appearances at conferences and events all around the globe, he spoke with the confidence of a salesman who had just what the world wanted -- and he did. Nvidia's graphics processing units, high powered computer processors packed with billions of transistors, are the central component behind what many believe is the next industrial revolution. 

The chipmaker's importance to global customers made Huang a worldwide celebrity. He frequently met with top U.S. and Chinese officials, and was regularly mobbed by adoring fans when he visited Taiwan, his birthplace and the global manufacturing hub of the chip industry. 

Then, on Sunday, Huang acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized for violating his family's and his employees' trust. That affair involved Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, which has been a major Nvidia customer and who U.S. intelligence officials believe is working for China's intelligence services. 

The Nvidia CEO also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a senior executive at Nvidia who runs the company's healthcare business, according to a person familiar with the matter. The New York Times earlier reported the second affair. Powell didn't respond to requests for comment. 

Shares of Nvidia were down almost 8% in premarket trading Thursday, extending a recent slide following the revelation that Nvidia's board was investigating Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang. The top executive, 63, is Nvidia's largest shareholder, owning about 3.6% of the company, and has become one of the richest people in the world. 

Huang, who had roughly 60 direct reports, has said he doesn't believe in succession planning and that leaders should continuously pass on knowledge and information as they have it. It wasn't immediately clear who would succeed him. 
Nvidia's latest proxy statement warns that it is "highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team" and that the failure to ensure effective succession planning could "hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success."

Taking a step back from the Jensen news.

This hits at a moment of broader AI anxiety: multi-year buildout costs, geopolitical delays on data centers, and the risk that new models reduce the need for expensive inference. All of it has fed the selloff.

None of it changes the underlying reality. We’re still early. Adoption is sub 1%, and the steep part of the inference S-curve is still ahead of us. 

Nvidia’s GPUs remain a step-function better than AMD’s, evidenced by ~
90% GPU market share even at a higher price.

The uncertainty in $NVDA creates a window for new capital to come in and benefit from the next several years of the AI buildout, of which Nvidia will account for about 50% of that cost.

posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
Jensen Huang’s resignation ends an era at NVIDIA and forces a stress test on the AI trade.

Huang wasn’t just a CEO. He was the face, the product visionary and the operator who turned NVIDIA into the $4T+ foundation of the AI boom. Key-man risk was always priced in at some level; today it is no longer theoretical. $NVDA stock is already down hard (10%+ in premarket) and the rest of the AI complex is feeling the spillover.

The near-term picture is messy. Leadership uncertainty, succession questions and the China-related overhang from the scandal create real noise. Colette Kress (long-time CFO, now interim CEO) and the existing leadership team provide operational continuity and the board has appointed Harvey Jones as its first Chair. Product roadmaps, CUDA lock-in and hyperscaler demand don’t disappear overnight. Still, the narrative premium from $NVDA is gone.

The setup for a multi-week rally is strong. AI stocks were already deeply oversold coming into this news after the recent sharp selloff. Technicals are washed out, sentiment is depressed and multiple strategists had already called the prior dip extreme. Forced selling and panic often exhaust quickly in these regimes. A relief bounce across the AI complex over the next several weeks looks highly probable as the dust settles.

The multi-month view is more nuanced. The AI infrastructure buildout itself is not over. Capex remains massive, data-centre demand is still the dominant growth driver and the underlying technology stack (accelerated computing, inference, networking) continues to expand. What changes is that NVIDIA must now prove it can execute without its founder-CEO narrative. Succession clarity, any regulatory/export fallout and whether the next permanent CEO can maintain the same cultural and technical intensity will decide if this is a healthy reset or the start of a longer period of relative underperformance versus the broader AI complex.

This is a classic “sell the rumor / buy the fact” environment for the trade. Oversold conditions favour a multi-week bounce. The multi-month case for AI stocks rests on whether the structural demand story can remain intact and companies with high margins, FCF and strong balance-sheets are likely to outperform. http://alphatarget.com

The market has staged a powerful snapback rally, but that doesn't mean the technical damage has been repaired.

We've seen a sharp rebound that forced shorts to cover, and now comes the real test: can buyers defend these gains, build higher lows, and establish a foundation for a sustainable advance?

*

After a massive selloff that erased the post-midterm gap, broke below $750, and tested the 200-day moving average, $SPY rebounded toward $762.50.

Now I'm watching $755.

Holding that level would be impressive and could allow the market to consolidate constructively.

A retest of $750 and change wouldn't necessarily destroy the setup, but sustained weakness below $750 could bring back choppy, difficult trading conditions.

*

$QQQ has staged a V-shaped recovery from roughly $647 to $695.57.

The question is whether that V can develop into a W-shaped bottom.

The immediate level to watch is $683, where yesterday's low and the 200-day moving average converge.

Holding above that area would demonstrate real commitment from buyers.

A shakeout toward $680 is possible, while a deeper pullback toward $667 could still establish a higher low and set up another advance into Thanksgiving.

*

$NVDA is a great example why you should follow a process instead of blindly buying big stocks.

#Nvidia has fallen sharply from $243, failed its breakout, broken its ascending channel, and remained below key short-term moving averages.

There were warning signs well before the latest controversy surrounding Jensen Huang.

The $164–$165 area is now critical. If #NVDA stays below it, $153 becomes the next potential downside target.

Don't buy a falling knife simply because it's Nvidia!

*

I'm holding a small position in $GOOGL for a potential gap-fill trade.

Despite the damaged chart, #Google could attract some rotation within the Mag Seven.

Ideally, it holds $285 and reclaims $296. A sustained move above $296 could open the door toward $300 or higher.

If the setup fails, I'll respect my stop and move on.

*

#Tesla remains trapped in a frustrating trading range despite its recent four-day recovery.

The key level for $TSLA now is $386. If buyers can defend it and build a base, another continuation setup could emerge.

But I'm skeptical. A failure to hold $386 could lead to a gap fill and another disappointing reversal for #TSLA.

*

Bottom line: if you missed the snapback rally, you haven't necessarily missed the opportunity.

The market needs time to rebuild. I'm watching whether SPY holds $755, $QQQ defends $683, and individual stocks begin reclaiming important moving averages.

Until we see that commitment, staying tactical, managing risk, and waiting for better setups makes more sense than chasing a rally that hasn't yet proven itself.

posts.text:
Why is $NBIS down -15% in pre-market? 🤔

The economics have never looked better.
Pre-tax profitable before the end of 2027.
100% pre-payments.

So why is the stock getting crushed on news that massively de-risks the business long-term?

1) Data center buildout delays
2) In my view, INSANELY low 2027 revenue guidance

First-glance gut reaction:

1) I don't mind the delays. They come from third-party partner projects, not Nebius's own builds, which are all on track. And going forward, 75%+ of projects will be their own.

2) The guidance makes no sense to me at first glance. It doesn't match the capacity they plan to bring online or the $/MW we're currently seeing. I'll study it in detail over the next 48 hours and run the math properly to make sense of it.

The ONLY ways I can explain it:
a) a massive sandbag (like MASSIVE!)
b) they expect very big delays in 2027 (doesn't sound like it from the call)
c) they're selling a huge share of capacity on long-term contracts (3-5 years) at much lower prices than expected -> this seems very possible, to de-risk the business by capping both the upside and the downside.

This was one of the most unusual quarters, in the sense that we got a ton of amazing new insights but also confirmation of very bad delays and low guidance. It's definitely a mixed bag of great and bad stuff. Not the usual pure bull porn.

Considering we went +15% into earnings yesterday, it seems expectations were higher. But let's see what the market thinks over the next few sessions. The Jensen news still seems to be a dark cloud over all AI infra stocks (except $AMD) right now.

Over the next few days, I will go much deeper into all the new info (there's a ton to break down!) and reserve the right to change my mind! I also think there's a very high chance the guidance is just ridiculously conservative.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Resigns as CEO

NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition

Jensen Huang Resigns
Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

The question before Nvidia's board is not whether he is great. It is whether he can still be trusted, and in a public company trust is not a sentiment. It is the entire basis on which strangers hand over their capital. It is the foundation of the fiduciary responsibility a CEO accepts when he takes the position.

No one is demanding sainthood. The standard here is far lower, and he failed it. Do not carry on a relationship with a woman US intelligence officials suspect of working for China's Ministry of State Security while your company is the chokepoint of American export controls. That is not sainthood. That is the floor for running a public company.

Thirty years of building earns gratitude. It does not earn immunity from the rules he set himself. The presumption belongs to founders who comply. He spent his.

posts.text:
Ian Buck (VP Hyperscale and high-performance computing) is the most likely Internal candidate.  

From Grok:  Buck is best known as the inventor of CUDA, $NVDA’s foundational software platform for general-purpose GPU computing.

He joined NVIDIA in 2004 after earning his PhD in computer science from Stanford University (thesis on stream computing on graphics hardware; advisor Pat Hanrahan). At Stanford he led development of Brook, a stream programming language that was a key precursor to general-purpose computing on GPUs (GPGPU). He also holds a BSE in computer science from Princeton University (summa cum laude, class of 1999).
In his current role, Buck leads the multi-billion-dollar datacenter business unit focused on AI and HPC products. He oversees AI hardware and software used by major hyperscalers and AI companies (including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI, and others), manages product development, partnerships, and go-to-market strategy, and is a direct report to CEO Jensen Huang. He has described the evolution from individual chips to full “AI factory” / rack-scale systems as a core focus.

Why he matters: CUDA turned GPUs into programmable accelerators for scientific computing and, later, deep learning and generative AI. It became the standard platform used by millions of developers and is widely viewed as a key element of NVIDIA’s competitive advantage (often called its “moat”) in AI computing. Buck has testified before the U.S. Congress on AI, advised the White House, and works on national AI supercomputers. He is frequently cited in industry discussions of NVIDIA’s leadership and has appeared in reporting on potential internal succession candidates.

He regularly speaks at events such as GTC, OCP, and HPC conferences on topics including GPU data centers, agentic AI, power efficiency, and full-stack AI infrastructure.

$NVDA (-4.4% AH):  Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him

Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, is already facing scrutiny over an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.

New York Times
Ryan MacTripp Mickle and Georgia Gee
Nov. 11, 2026, 4:55 p.m. ET

Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.

The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.

Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.

Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The New York Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.

This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefingon his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.

China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up.

Nvidia declined to provide a statement. Ms. Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

posts.text:
$NBIS reports tomorrow before the open. $CRWV print last night suggested demand isn't the problem for neoclouds. 

For Nebius, the question is execution: can it ramp fast enough to hit a very aggressive year-end target?

What I need to see:

1. The ARR ramp ARR was $3B in June, and the year-end guide is $7–9B. Q3 exit ARR needs to land around $4.5B+ to keep that credible. If they cut this, nothing else matters.

2. Revenue and guide Consensus is ~$905M for Q3. The FY guide of $3.0–3.4B implies $1.1–1.5B in Q4. Hold it or raise it.

3. Connected power The guide is 800 MW–1 GW by year-end. I want Q3 connected power around 675 MW or higher, and no slippage at new sites.

4. Microsoft Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight of Nebius projects. I want management to address it directly and confirm the New Jersey deployment is on schedule.

5. Funding mix In Q2 they had $8B of cash and $9B+ of customer prepayments covering 50–60% of capex, but also raised ~$2.8B by selling stock (ATM). Against a $20–25B capex year, I want prepayment coverage holding, more asset-backed debt and less dilution.

Nebius is far less levered than CoreWeave. What it has to prove now is on-time delivery, because that's exactly where the Microsoft headlines hit.

You could buy 100 shares of $AMZN right now for about $26,600.

Or you could sell the $250 put expiring January 15, 2027 and get paid roughly $720 to wait.

Amazon sold off after its October 29 earnings report. Earnings missed estimates, and management said it expects to spend meaningfully more on capital projects in 2027 than this year's roughly $220B. The stock fell as low as $229 the next day and has rallied about 16% from that low. It now trades around $266, about 7% below its 52-week high.

The business keeps growing. AWS revenue grew 39% to $46B last quarter, with a $578B backlog.

A stock that moves like that pays you to wait. Implied volatility on this put is about 33%, and the $250 strike sits about 6% below the current price.

Amazon's next earnings report is expected in early February, after this put expires.

The plan: close at 50% of max profit by buying the put back around $3.60. That's half the credit, often in a fraction of the time.

If $AMZN drops toward $250 and the thesis still holds, you could roll down and out for more credit. If you get assigned, your cost basis is $242.80, about 8.7% below today's price, and you could start selling covered calls.

The setup: $250 strike, 0.29 delta, 65 days to expiration, 2.9% return on capital (about 16% annualized).

When I make a trade, my thinking is never about being right or even wrong. It's about risk vs. reward. I call it Bell Curve Thinking. I ask myself, if I make this trade 1000 times, does it come out a winner. Is it likely that the trade's upside is at least 2-3X the my stop?  If I get those right, the rest takes care of itself.
My most recent $SPY short is a perfect example. The stock fell 5X my stop. I had the opportunity to capture 5Rs. But that's precisely what afforded me to hold for a bigger move while improving my stop to breakeven. I made that decision based on the odds at the time.  If I turn out to be wrong... nothing lost. posts.text:
My memo to our clients this morning:

Yesterday, we doubled our already profitable S&P 500 short exposure because we believe the potential for further downside remains worth the miniscule risk we are taking. Our original position has been completely de-risked, and the additional shares were added using what we call an "add and reduce" technique", allowing us to increase exposure without materially increasing overall risk. This puts us in our favorite position: large profit potential with very small risk.

The Nasdaq triggered a follow-through day. We take that seriously, but now we need to see whether the rally can gain traction or if distribution rears its head in the coming days. With a good-sized hedge bet in place, we are open to adding some longs as they meet our criteria. Currently, the list is small, but there are a few names we are considering. Refer to our Focus List for current names.

Many of yesterday's biggest winners were in the AI/technology stocks that had been beaten down and severely oversold. CoreWeave is an especially good illustration. It exploded 24.7% yesterday, but closed at $60.77 versus a 52-week high of $138.2 - still down about 56% below its high. IREN gained 5.6% but closed at $20.84 against a $70.71 high, still roughly 71% below its high. Those are enormous rallies but occurring inside badly damaged charts. Most of yesterday's tech stock rallies occurred within strong downtrends.

Macro and policy risks still argue for staying selective rather than chasing a market with very few sound stock setups. Sticky inflation, the prospect of additional Fed rate hikes, rising long-term interest rates, and increasing talk of regulation surrounding AI and data centers are all reasons to remain cautious about a nascent rally that, so far, has largely been a rebound from an oversold condition.

Interest rates remain particularly important. After pulling back from an overbought condition, the 10-year yield has started turning higher again, while the 1-year yield jumped sharply. That is not exactly the backdrop you want to see if you’re looking for expanding equity valuations and a sustained risk-on move.

Investors Intelligence bulls fell sharply to 37.0% from 42.6% last week, the lowest bullish reading since early April, when bulls reached 33.3%. That's a significant reversal from just six weeks ago, when bulls stood at 57.7% as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were hitting highs. That peak was one of three readings above the 55% danger level that historically signals elevated risk.

At the same time, bears jumped to 24.1% from 18.5%, the highest bearish reading since April. The shift is encouraging from a contrary-sentiment standpoint, particularly after several weeks when bearish readings remained unusually low.

Sentiment is definitely moving in the right direction, but we don't believe the ratio of bulls to bears has reached the extreme normally associated with a major contrary buy signal. For now, we view the change primarily as a directional indication. Optimism is being wrung out and pessimism is building as stocks retreat from their highs. That's constructive, but it isn't necessarily capitulation. We would like to see sentiment deteriorate further before treating it as a powerful contrary signal.

A follow-through day is important piece of evidence, but it is not a license to blindly rush back into the market. The real confirmation will come from the market of stocks - better price action, expanding leadership and a proliferation of quality setups emerging from sound bases.

For now, we are taking a measured approach. We will look to add some long exposure incrementally as individual stocks prove themselves. We strongly advise you only get aggressive on the heels of portfolio traction. The weight of evidence suggests that we are not yet completely out of the woods. Let the market earn your exposure. For now, maintain short (hedge) exposure and adhere to stops.

posts.text:
NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition
November 12, 2026
Jensen Huang Resigns

Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO

Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”  

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” 

Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

quoted.text: The way this normally goes is that an interim CEO gets named. Then they go through a selection process of internal and external candidates and sometimes the interim CEO gets the job.

He says the job of a board member is not to add value or give advice. It is to replace the CEO.

For anyone who hasn't heard about this yet: ICE showed up at the front door of Dr. Ann Lawani in Lodi, California, while she was still in her pajamas, shackled her at the wrists, waist, and ankles, and shipped her all the way to a detention center in Louisiana.

She’s a frontline nurse who worked through the worst of COVID, directs the master's nursing program at the University of San Francisco (overseeing 230+ nursing students), and takes care of her 83-year-old dad.

When her family and lawyer tried to find out where she was taken, ICE’s online locator came back with "0 results." It turns out ICE quietly changed its policy the day before her arrest to stop listing thousands of detainees in the public database, so her family had no idea where she was for days while she was bounced from Stockton to Bakersfield to El Paso to Louisiana.

DHS put out a statement claiming she had a 2013 removal order, but they conveniently left out that on the *exact same day* in 2013, an immigration judge granted her Withholding of Removal blocking her deportation to Nigeria because she faced persecution there. 

She has zero criminal record, has checked in with ICE for 13 years, and has a valid federal work permit through 2029. Because they legally can't send her to Nigeria, Rep. Josh Harder says ICE has been trying to quietly deport her to an undisclosed third country behind her lawyer's back.

Full write-up and breakdown of what happened here:

Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

Seeing LLMs write code makes many expect the same speed in biology. But bio can only iterate at the speed of life. That includes generating the data AI needs to eventually simulate life! The more optimistic we are about AI, the more urgent it is to start the slow work now.

posts.name: Ruxandra Teslo 🧬
posts.text:
What are the visions of the post-AGI future in San Francisco? Many think we're all going to die, but even the "positive" visions seem rather dystopian. Here, I wrote about "handoverism," which involves handing control of the future to an AGI God, with humans outside the loop.
https://ruxandrabio.substack.com/p/handing-over-humanity

We are on the cusp of RSI or recursive self-improvement: this means that AI systems can self-improve, without the need for human intervention. This means our world stands to be transformed in what many call “the singularity”. I moved to SF around three weeks ago and one of the things I have been trying to understand is where we are heading, at least according to those developing the tech.

The worst scenarios are plainly bleak: all of us, or vast numbers of us, die. But what is striking to me is how little reassurance even some of the happiest scenarios offer. But one common and ostensibly optimistic vision is known as “handoverism”: humanity cedes control of its future to a godlike AI and we become the comfortably maintained inhabitants of a civilisation whose direction is no longer ours to decide. It is difficult to see what democracy would mean in such a world, or where the consent of most of humanity to the instantiation of such a regime enters the picture.

The permanent displacement of human labour is treated almost as a given. At the same time, there is scarcely any satisfying answer to the question of how we might remain useful to one another. Even our relationships seem uncertain. The promised utopia looks to me much closer to a kind of dystopia.

“It’s not my preferred outcome,” someone working at one of the big labs told me, “but once we achieve superintelligence, which we cannot stop at this point, I cannot see any other option for where humanity will go.” Then, after a pause, he added: “It is still much better than what I actually fear most, which is that we might all die.”

He sounded resigned, as if the question of what humans would be for (apparently not much?) had already been settled somewhere else and by someone else. All that remains, it seems, is to wait for this pre-destined fate to unfold before our eyes.

But I do not think that is the case. I believe we always have a choice and that we should try and steer this technology in a way that maintains our agency and control. And even if that looks hard and daunting, the immensity of the stakes here make it worth trying at least.

I do not know whether the handoverist vision will come to pass. That the people building this technology consider it plausible, and often desirable, guarantees nothing: proximity to a technology does not correlate that well with predicting its impact on society.

But they are the ones closest to it, and what they say deserves to be at least taken seriously. The rest of society, including some very intelligent people, has been far too quick to wave these scenarios away and not even get involved in the debate. Whether or not the belief is correct, it is sincerely held, and it is not “marketing hype.” I am writing this because I think it is high time that more people, inside San Francisco and out, engaged with the arguments about what our future will look like, and answered them.

Jeff Bezos was married to MacKenzie Scott for 25 years.

Bezos and MacKenzie were reportedly longtime friends with Lauren Sánchez and her husband, Patrick Whitesell, who actually introduced Lauren to Bezos.

Then Bezos reportedly had an affair with Lauren while both were still married.

The affair became public in 2019, and both couples eventually divorced.

Bezos remained Amazon's CEO until 2021, then became Executive Chairman.

In 2025, Bezos married Lauren in a lavish wedding in Venice.

And Amazon has been doing just fine. The stock is now more than 3x its January 2019 price.

Not bringing this up to say anything bad about Bezos. My point is, sometimes that's just how life works.

I think we are all so shocked and disappointed about Jensen because we have admired and respected him so much for so many years.

We probably put him on too high a pedestal and expected him to be almost perfect.

But at the end of the day, Jensen is human too. He has his flaws, just like the rest of us.

We don't have to agree with everything he does, but that doesn't mean we should forget everything he has accomplished.

I still respect Jensen, and I'm still thankful for what he has built. 

Also, I don't think it's end of the world for NVDA. Jensen doesn't have to be the CEO to still lead the company.

posts.text:
Dude just got profiled by the WSJ. Quite a story.

Christian Lamarco, 31. Went to a small Christian college in Pennsylvania with no Wall Street recruiting pipeline.

Once drove to Carnegie Mellon to compete against Ivy Leaguers in a stock-picking contest. Finished second. Won $100.

Cold-emailed his research to hedge funds, landed a job at a Chicago long-short fund, then quit in 2019 with just a few months of savings to start Culper Research.

Moved to NYC, working out of a Brooklyn apartment. His team? Just two analysts.

They started investigating Nvidia last year, then gave up. They doubted three guys could uncover something Wall Street had missed about the world's most valuable company.

Picked it back up in March.

Interviewed former Nvidia employees, dug through corporate filings in Singapore and Malaysia, examined scrubbed code, even studied YouTube footage outside a Taiwanese noodle shop.

May 13: After a sleepless night, a bagel and a cigarette, he published a 40-page short report flagging Nvidia’s China exposure and Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang.

The next day, Nvidia hit an all-time high.

Nobody cared.

Six months later, the story blew up…

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Sixty Years Above 2%, and Now the Fed Panics?

Services always run hot. Goods are doing their job. Oil is the shock.

Wall Street and the Fed are freaking out over services inflation, a number that has run above 2% for most of modern history. Since 1960, PCE services prices have topped 2% in 86% of months. Even in the 2010s, the decade we now remember as "too low" inflation, services ran above 2% three-quarters of the time. Today they sit at 3.5%, a flat 3.3 to 3.5% band for a year and well below the 6% peak of 2023.

The 2% target was never met because services behaved. It was met because goods deflated. From 1995 to 2019, core goods CPI ran at or below 2% in 96% of months and below zero 41% of the time. In the 2010s, the median was negative.

Look at the latest CPI. Core goods are running at just 0.7% year over year and rose only 0.2% in October. They've drifted down from 1.4% over the past year. Used cars are down 3.3% and new vehicles are up 0.7%. Tariff-sensitive items like furniture and appliances ticked up for the month, but furnishings are just 0.2% over the year. This is the old pattern returning: goods anchor, services carry.

The 4.6% jump in all-goods inflation is the oil shock. Energy goods are up 35%, and gasoline is up 37%. That's a negative supply shock, and the Fed's overnight rate can't drill a well, reopen a shipping lane or end a war.

Hiking into this mistakes supply for demand. Higher rates choke housing supply, which keeps shelter sticky, while Main Street and the cyclical economy outside AI pay the price.

The Fed is a sledgehammer, not a fine-tuning machine. Look past the oil shock, respect a century of services history, and let productivity do the work.

posts.name: Sahil Bloom
posts.text:
After I posted this, I got asked a lot of questions about improving marathon performance.

I think there are two things that matter for running a faster marathon:

1. Preparation
2. Execution

Here's how I think about each one:

(stream of consciousness, so pardon any errors)

1. Preparation

This is just how well you prepared for the race.

What did your training look like? Were you prepared for the distance? Did you have enough confidence built up from your training block to go into the race feeling good about your ability to execute?

There are plenty of smart coaches on here that can give you better advice than me, but my staples here would be:

- 1 weekly long run
- 1 weekly track workout
- 3-4 easy runs

Long run has progression work or intervals to prepare your body (and mind) for the faster paces you'll have to run on race day on tired legs.

Track workouts generally focus on middle distance intervals (800m, 1200m, 1600m) on medium rest intervals (90-120s). For me, I view this work as acclimating my body and nervous system to paces significantly faster than what I'll have to run on race day.

Nutrition matters during preparation, too. Consuming enough calories, particularly in the form of carbs, to fuel yourself to perform. Under-eating during training is a great way to get hurt (or experience massive muscle loss). The nutrition part extends into executing your pre-race carb load during the 2-3 days leading up to the race as well.

2. Execution

I break this into 4 components:

1. Pacing
2. Nutrition
3. Hydration
4. Mindset

Pacing is just about how well you execute your pacing plan for the race. If it's mostly flat, ideally an easy negative split, where you start out below marathon pace target and slowly get faster. If it's a hilly course, planning and executing around those climbs.

Having completely screwed this up in my first three marathons (and then nailed it in my recent one), I know how impactful it is on how you feel later in the race.

Avoiding the adrenaline-driven surge early is the whole game for a novice. You pay for it later. Trust me.

Nutrition is about the carbs you consume during the race. The biggest mistake I've made in the past was under-consuming carbs during my long runs and races.

You have to train the way you're going to play on race day. Practice your nutrition. Test the gels and find what your body tolerates and responds to best.

Then, don't do anything new on race day. 

My strategy for this was one gel every 30 minutes, each with 50g carbs (I used Carbs Fuel because I liked it and it didn't destroy my stomach).

Practicing on your training runs also avoids making dumb rookie mistakes (like I made) around dropping gels or realizing your cold fingers can't tear them.

Hydration is about the fluids you consume during the race. This is what I screwed up during my DNF in September.

You need to tailor your fluid consumption to the race day conditions. Higher temperature / dew point means more fluid needs. There are precise ways to figure this out, but the best way is to just experiment during your long runs and make sure you match your race day approach to what has worked.

Personally, I've found that fluids are extremely overrated on cold days but have an exponentially increasing importance as temperatures tick up.

I consumed just two 14oz bottles with electrolytes during my marathon last weekend. But if it had been 20 degrees warmer, I would have cramped and blown up only consuming that amount.

Mindset is about how you approach the race and distance itself. How you break it up in your mind. How you navigate the inevitable random dark thoughts during a race. How you respond to the little pains and cramps that strike.

To be honest, I think this one is deeply intertwined with the first three execution components.

It's very easy to have a good mindset when you're feeling great because you're executing on pacing, nutrition, and hydration. You start passing people. That feels good. You feel s

Some trivia or something most of you would never know abour me. 
In the 1980's, I manufactured and distributed one of the earlier widely commercialized blackjack strategy cards. It was on credit card plastic and meant to be handheld to help players with basic strategy. This was one of the earlier versions meant for single deck play. It was available in vending machines and gift shops in Atlantic City at the airport and on the boardwalk. 
At the time, I also wrote articles for a magazine called gambling times. In exchange, they traded me advertising space for the Blackjack Card.  I was just 22 years old. 
My wife just found it while cleaning out a closet. 😎

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
The Dutch, my fellow citizens, are going absolutely berserk over a new tax plan.

Not just because of what's in it, but also because of the extraordinarily amateurish way it has been put together.

The Netherlands has a minority government, meaning governing parties can shop around for parliamentary support to secure a majority.

The tax plan has been changed over and over again, and each time it gets a little crazier.

While its contents are raising plenty of eyebrows, the process of reaching an agreement is becoming downright laughable.

What the Bloomberg snippet doesn't tell you is that the Council of State, the government's most important independent adviser, has strongly argued against it.

The proposal also includes taxing unrealized gains on crypto and precious metals, potentially extending to certain pension-related investments, not shown in the Bloomberg snippet.

And then there's the Dutch Tax Administration, which has already been at the center of a disastrous benefits fraud scandal. It has repeatedly warned that it simply cannot implement the government's ever-changing plans.

So we have a government pushing ahead with a controversial tax plan, its most important adviser raising serious objections, and the tax authority saying it cannot execute it.

Dutch politics is making a complete fool of itself.

To all non-Dutch readers and followers: what do you make of this? How does it compare with the tax policies and political decision-making in your own country?

Examples are very welcome.

En la actualidad conviven dos shocks a distinta velocidad. 

El energético es inflacionista y rápido, y su efecto dura más por el refino, mientras que el shock chino es deflacionista, lento y estructural, y llega a través de los bienes.

La explicación es que China exporta deflación en bienes mientras la energía y los salarios sostienen la inflación en servicios, y aunque Brooks acierta en la dirección del shock chino, puede sobrestimar la holgura al medirla con la tendencia previa a la pandemia, porque después de cinco años de shocks de oferta, la capacidad productiva también es menor.

US small businesses are signaling more inflation ahead:

The proportion of US small firms planning to raise prices over the next 3 months rose +6 percentage points in October, to 37%, the most since July 2022.

By comparison, this figure did not exceed 30% between 2009 and 2019.

Furthermore, 33% of small firms raised prices over the last 3 months, the 3rd-highest reading since March 2023.

Meanwhile, 17% of business owners pointed to inflation as their single most important problem, up from 12% a year ago.

Small businesses are preparing for further price hikes as inflationary pressures mount.

European Gas Rises as Cool Weather, Outages Draw Down Stockpiles

European natural gas extended gains for a third day as cold weather in parts of the region contributes to accelerated drawdowns of already thin inventories.

Benchmark futures gained as much as 4.7% on Thursday. As heating demand increases, withdrawals of gas are occurring at a faster pace than at the same time last year, data from Gas Infrastructure Europe show. Meanwhile, unplanned outages in Norway are further tightening supply.

Europe entered this year’s heating season with lower-than-usual stockpiles, after the Middle East war choked off liquefied natural gas flows that previously accounted for a fifth of global exports. Accelerated drawdowns early in the season risk leaving the region more exposed during later winter months, and could also make it harder to replenish the buffer next year. (Bloomberg)

Core CPI inflation surged to a 3-month annualized rate of +3.75% in October, its highest reading since April 2024.

At the same time, core services less shelter inflation, also known as Supercore CPI and closely monitored by the Fed, rose to a 3-month annualized rate of +5.45%, its highest since mid-2024.

The weighted proportion of CPI components rising at an annualized rate above 2% soared to 76% last month, the largest percentage since August 2022.

The Fed's fight against inflation is far from over.

quoted.text:
As I said in the note, not my favorite model to use for tariffs.

On your issue, the fall in tariff-related equipment prices in FRB/US is an artifact of consumer prices up, it doesn't want overall prices up by as much, so it forces the residual into investment prices.

Plus the cost to a business is the equipment plus the customs duty, and FRB/US doesn't handle that.

Overall capital goods paid about one-third of tariffs, inputs up in price, and past episodes seem to have reduced investment.

That said, tariffs affect different industries very differently and in some your effect would predominate. Unfortunately FRB/US doesn't have industries so can't model that--why it's not my favorite model for this.

posts.name: Jason Furman
posts.text:
A clever piece, literally running FRB/US on tariffs does result in higher investment--as John correctly notes.

From the very last page of The Everything Code. Out now.

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
The United States holds more than 8,100 metric tons of gold. 

When was the last time anyone physically counted it all?  

I ask because of what happened in the Netherlands. As I explain in the (Dutch) post below, the Dutch finance minister barely asks how the country’s €72 billion in gold is checked. 

The Dutch central bank visits its foreign vaults to inspect the gold. The external auditor appointed by the minister doesn’t come along, and relies on written confirmation from the central banks that hold it.  

By 2008, auditors had physically counted the gold in every deep-storage compartment at Fort Knox, Denver, and West Point over several years, but the public audit record gives no date for a full physical count of the entire U.S. gold reserve.

Auditors have relied on intact seals at the Mint and written confirmation from the New York Fed, but if you own gold for the day the financial system falters, wouldn’t you want someone to open the vault every now and then?

quoted.text:
€72 miljard aan goud. Maar de politiek kijkt weg?

€72 miljard aan goud. 612,4 ton, verspreid over vier kluizen in New York, Ottawa, Londen en Zeist. En het ministerie van Financiën heeft er vrijwel geen zicht op.

Dat is de harde conclusie van de Algemene Rekenkamer. De accountant van het ministerie gaat niet mee bij de controlebezoeken in het buitenland. Daardoor kan Financiën niet met zekerheid zeggen of het gerapporteerde goud er fysiek ligt. Minister Heinen vertrouwt erop dat DNB het goed op orde heeft.

Serieus?

In al onze presentaties zeggen we dat bij goud, en sowieso bij schaarse activa, echt bezit telt. Als je goud aanhoudt als bescherming tegen het haperen van het financiële systeem, precies zoals De Nederlandschse Bank doet, kun je maar beter zeker weten dat het er daadwerkelijk ligt. En dat het veilig is.

Dat het ministerie daar zo weinig aandacht voor heeft, zegt veel over de checks-and-balances, zoals het FD terecht opmerkt. Maar het zegt ook iets over het (on)begrip van het departement van de rol van goud in het financiële systeem.

Van elke fondsbeheerder en financiële instelling wordt tegenwoordig een massa aan informatie gevraagd. Compliance, regelgeving, continue monitoring. Het daadwerkelijk vaststellen van bezit lijkt me daarbij toch een van de meest fundamentele controles.

Zoals ik al vaker heb meegegeven, onder meer met deze foto, gaan wij toch graag zelf periodiek ‘even’ in Zwitserland kijken of ons goud nog in de kluis ligt.

Het gebrek aan belang

posts.name: Meb Faber
posts.text: Very important take, even though inflation is down, it's still at a higher plateau and that's what people care about.

quoted.text:
We have record GDP, record stock prices, record wealth, near record median real wages, etc. So why is sentiment so bad? 

It's mostly what I would call a "price level shock". People view raises as something they earned and price increases as something done to them, so “real incomes are up” doesn’t always register as a positive.

Economists measure inflation as a rate of change (and it's about average now). Consumers feel it as a *cumulative* price shock (and that's near a 30 year high). Gas being at $5 might be a low rate of inflation, but we remember clearly when it was $3. That cumulative effect impacts sentiment.  

Check out these charts. It doesn't explain all of sentiment, but it explains a lot of it. When cumulative inflation is low sentiment is good. When it's up sentiment is bad.

posts.name: Jay Parsons
posts.text:
If you don't see the connection between high interest rates and reduced housing supply, here is Exhibit 192: Camden just canceled two big apartment development projects because the math no longer works.

CEO Alex Jessett on recent earnings call: "We were hoping that we'd find ways to make it so that they did work. And the reality is we just couldn't get there."

One was in Nashville, the other Denver. In Nashville, it was an urban site in the Gulch. Camden ended up buying an existing apartment property next-door to its development site. That acquisition cost $370k per unit compared to development that would cost $600k per unit.

In fairness, the build-vs-buy gap isn't that large everywhere (especially in low-density areas). But Camden's story reflects a harsh reality for developers today, as they confront the realities of rate hikes:

1) Debt costs are going up, and builders rely on debt.

2) Higher rates = lesser value. Apartment values are down about 5% due to rate hike. As a developer, your costs are going up at the same time the value of what you're building is going down. That's a formula that hurts development.
